facility_roles.quote: Figure 4 shows the layout of the slow-extracted intense proton beam from the Alternating Gradient Synchrotron (AGS) at Brookhaven, during the period 1973-1974. Our experiment (No. 598) was located in a specially designed beam line (the A-line).

intervals.label: proposal
intervals.locator: Ting Nobel Lecture, section I (caption text of Figure 3, the proposal page)
intervals.note: Ting presented the proposal in the spring of 1972 (A4 season: middle month April); he says he decided on the experiment in 1971. The extracted text drops the e⁺e⁻ superscripts.
intervals.quote: it gives some of the reasons I presented, in the spring of 1972, for performing an e + e experiment in a proton beam rather than in a photon beam

intervals.label: discovery run
intervals.note: Month precision. Tune-ups ran from April to August 1974; the J peak was found at the end of August. The end is the day Ting changed the spectrometer to start a new experiment.
intervals.quote: In April 1974, we finished the set-up of the experiment and started bringing an intense-proton beam into the area.

intervals.label: completed
intervals.note: This record covers the discovery configuration of E598 only: on 7 November 1974 the group reconfigured the spectrometer for a new experiment, whose later history is not recorded here.
intervals.quote: On Thursday, 7 November, we made a major change in the spectrometer (see Fig. 13) to start the new experiment to search for more particles.

quantity.note: The abstract of the discovery paper calls the AGS a "30-GeV alternating-gradient synchrotron".
quantity.quote: for an incident proton energy of 28.3 GeV
even though we had 10,000 tons of concrete shielding blocks

name: AGS E598 (J-particle discovery run)
notes: Only the Brookhaven side is recorded, as assigned: the SLAC discovery of the same particle (Mark I at SPEAR) belongs to the colliders stream.
The experiment number is given in Ting's lecture: "Our experiment (No. 598)". The MIT Laboratory for Nuclear Science group is on the author list; no collaboration record is created.

The J paper abstract and the BNL Nobel page both place the discovery at the AGS; the Nobel citation (1976) is shared with Burton Richter "for their pioneering work in the discovery of a heavy elementary particle of a new kind".

physics_goals.quote: to search for more heavy photons by detecting their e + e - decay modes up to a mass (m) of 5 GeV
physics_goals.value: Search for heavy photons by detecting their e⁺e⁻ decay modes up to a mass of 5 GeV

summary.plain: Samuel Ting's MIT group used a precise electron-positron pair spectrometer on Brookhaven's AGS proton beam and, in late summer 1974, saw a sharp peak at 3.1 GeV: a new heavy particle he called J. This record covers the Brookhaven side only; SLAC found the same particle as psi.
summary.technical: Fixed-target p + Be → e⁺e⁻ + X with a pair spectrometer in the AGS A-line: set-up finished April 1974, tune-up April-August, a narrow e⁺e⁻ peak at 3.1 GeV found at the end of August 1974, published as Phys. Rev. Lett. 33, 1404 (2 December 1974).

unique_capabilities.quote: by measuring the e+e− mass spectrum with a precise pair spectrometer at the Brookhaven National Laboratory's 30-GeV alternating-gradient synchrotron
unique_capabilities.value: A precise e⁺e⁻ pair spectrometer on the AGS proton beam
